sections.text:
I'm mapping out the five matplotlib charts generated from Excel workbooks, starting with the delta chart that plots call and put option deltas across different strike prices and time horizons, with separate curves for near and far expiration dates.

Continuing with gamma, which shows the rate of delta change — a bell curve that peaks near the strike price, with the near-term gamma spiking dramatically higher and narrower than the far-term version, illustrating the gamma explosion effect as expiration approaches.

Then there's the IV skew chart simulating equity-style volatility skew with a quadratic and linear adjustment to the at-the-money volatility across different strikes.

For theta, I'm looking at the time decay per day for calls, which forms a negative valley deepest at-the-money where decay accelerates sharply near expiry, while the far-term theta is shallower and spreads across a wider range of spot prices.

Now examining vega, which measures sensitivity to volatility changes — it peaks near-the-money in a bell shape, but behaves opposite to gamma across time: longer-dated options have much larger vega (they're pure volatility instruments), while short-dated options have minimal vega since they're dominated by gamma effects. The charts use consistent parameters across all greeks: strike at 100, 5% rates, 30% volatility, comparing 30-day versus 365-day expirations.

The pedagogical framework ties everything together through time's effect on each greek — near-term (red dashed) versus far-term (blue solid) curves, with ATM reference lines and moneyness labels for both calls and puts. The deeper insight is that delta becomes nearly binary near expiration (the S-curve flattens into a step function), gamma is literally the slope of delta with respect to spot price, and gamma and theta form a fundamental trade-off encoded in the Black-Scholes model itself — when gamma spikes, theta collapses, and vice versa.

The BSM PDE itself reveals the time-scaling asymmetry: vega scales with √T while gamma scales with 1/√T, so near expiry gamma dominates as the weapon of choice, while far out vega becomes critical. IV skew lives in strike-space, not spot-space, capturing the market's embedded crash risk. Put-call parity differentiated gives us the relationship between put and call deltas.

Now I'm thinking about how to rebuild this as a single-file HTML web app that integrates all these visualizations and insights — staying true to the established design language with the parchment background, teal and terracotta accents, and Noto Serif SC typography, all wrapped in dense, conclusion-first Chinese prose that matches his analytical style.

The key upgrade here is making everything interactive: live parameter sliders for strike, rate, volatility, and time horizons that drive all five charts simultaneously in real-time, replacing the old Excel macro workflow that required constant re-runs. One unified parameter panel controls all the Greeks across the board, consolidating what used to be five separate workbooks with redundant inputs. The dual near/far curve structure, ATM reference lines, and dual moneyness labeling stay intact to preserve the original analytical framework.

For the implementation, I'm deciding between canvas and SVG for the charts—canvas is faster but SVG gives me crisp lines and hover interactions more naturally. With 200 points across 2-4 curves per chart, SVG performance is solid, so I'll go that route and add a crosshair readout for exact values on hover, plus a time scrubber to animate the Greeks as days-to-expiration decay from 365 down.

The real pedagogical win is letting users watch how delta, gamma, theta, and vega evolve dynamically rather than freezing two snapshots. I'm also planning insight annotations for each chart in dense Chinese prose following his conclusion-first style, and possibly a unified comparison view highlighting the gamma-theta mirror relationship and gamma-vega time asymmetry.

For the overall structure, I'm keeping it single-file HTML with his established palette and Noto Serif SC typography, starting with a header containing the title and 导语.

The core architecture centers on a global parameter console with sliders for K, r, σ, T_near, T_far plus a time scrubber for animation control, then five chart sections each with the original SVG faithful to his design (red-dashed near, blue far, ATM dotted line, dual moneyness labels, gridlines), hover crosshairs, and insight prose panels. I'm also adding a synthesis section that visualizes the BSM PDE identity showing the gamma-theta mirror relationship. Vega chart alongside the others, then an IV skew visualization using strike as the x-axis while keeping spot and ATM vol as independent parameters. I'll add a synthesis section showing how ATM Greeks diverge across time (gamma scaling as 1/√T while vega scales as √T) plus the underlying PDE decomposition. For interactivity, I'm planning a time scrubber that animates the near-term curve collapsing toward expiration, with hover crosshairs across all charts and live slider updates.

I need to implement the core Black-Scholes math functions in JavaScript—normal CDF using the Abramowitz-Stegun approximation, normal PDF, and all the Greeks (delta, gamma, theta, vega) plus the IV skew formula. I'm hand-rolling SVG generation for each chart with axes, gridlines, curves, ATM markers, and a hover layer. The design uses a parchment background with a teal color scheme.

For the font, I'm using Noto Serif SC from Google Fonts with fallbacks to local Chinese serif fonts since CDN access might be blocked in his region. The writing style follows conclusion-first structure typical of Chinese business communication. For the curves, I'm mapping the original blue/red-dashed convention to teal solid for long-term and terracotta dashed for near-term, keeping the visual metaphor of cool colors for distant time horizons and warm for immediate.

Now I'm working through the precise Black-Scholes formulas: Delta uses the standard d1 calculation with a stock price range from 0.5K to 1.5K across 240 points for smoothness, Gamma follows the probability density formula across 0.7K to 1.3K, and Theta for calls incorporates the daily decay with the risk-free rate component. I'm treating the call Greeks as the representative case.

I'll add a Call/Put toggle for Theta to expose both branches that the original script computed, keeping it faithful while giving users the flexibility to switch. Vega stays consistent across both option types, and the IV skew follows a quadratic-linear model across the 0.75K to 1.25K range.

For the synthesis charts, I'm plotting the at-the-money term structure by holding S equal to K and showing how Gamma and Vega evolve across time horizons starting from roughly one day out.  I'll normalize each metric to its maximum value to highlight the scaling laws—Gamma decays as 1/√T while Vega grows as √T and Theta decays as −1/√T. I'm also overlaying Gamma and negative Theta scaled together to demonstrate their near-perfect correlation, since the dominant theta term is essentially −½σ²S²Γ.

The PDE constraint ties everything together: Θ_annual + ½σ²S²Γ + rSΔ − rV = 0. For the visualization, I'm adding synchronized crosshairs across all four spot-space charts so hovering over a strike price on one chart highlights the corresponding point on gamma, delta, theta, and vega simultaneously.

I'm structuring the layout with a max width around 1200px, placing charts in cards against an aged-paper background with subtle borders, and keeping a sticky console at the top with the adjustment sliders. For the section headers, I'll use classical Chinese chapter numbering like "第一图 Delta" or Greek glyphs to match his aesthetic preferences from previous projects. Each Greek letter section will have dense, conclusion-first prose written for a sophisticated options trader familiar with SpotGamma.

Now I'm detailing Delta: it's not a probability approximation but rather the replicating portfolio's position size; as time passes, the S-curve compresses into a step function where at expiration Delta only takes values of 0 or 1. Near-term contracts show extreme price sensitivity around ATM (that sensitivity is Gamma), while longer-dated contracts have their Delta flattened by time decay. The put-call relationship gives Put Delta = Call Delta − 1, and the four curves actually represent just two underlying curves shifted against each other.

For Gamma, I'm explaining it as the density of optionality itself—a bell curve peaking at ATM that collapses toward ATM as expiration approaches, with near-term contracts showing dramatically higher peaks than longer-dated ones. The formula shows how Gamma depends on the standard normal density, stock price, volatility, and time to expiration.

The square root of time in the denominator reveals Gamma scales inversely with √T at ATM, which explains the extreme behavior of zero-DTE options. For market makers this is a hedging frequency map; for buyers it's a convexity price list. Call and Put Gamma are identical because optionality is direction-agnostic.

Theta is fundamentally Gamma's cost—the curve mirrors Gamma inverted and scaled by the volatility term. The steepest time decay hits near-term ATM options, while deep ITM or OTM positions barely decay since they carry minimal Gamma. There's also a small financing cost component tied to the risk-free rate and strike.

Vega shares Gamma's bell shape and ATM peak, but the time structure inverts completely—√T appears in the numerator here, making longer-dated options the Vega playground while near-term is Gamma's domain. This temporal asymmetry is exactly what calendar spreads exploit: sell near-term Gamma, buy far-term Vega.

IV Skew breaks the constant volatility assumption and plots Greeks against strike instead. Equity options typically show a characteristic "smirk"—a smile pattern with a left skew where lower strikes have elevated implied volatility. 关键是让这五张图通过共享参数控制台（K、r、σ、T_near、T_far）和同步光标来联动，而不是简单地并排放置——它们本质上是同一个函数在不同维度的投影。我在构建一个交互式仪表板，包含参数滑块、五个SVG图表、跨图表的同步十字光标以及时间衰减动画，同时保留原始的公式、默认值（K=100、r=5%、σ=30%、30/365天）和双视角标签。

为了真正整合，我会让IV图表的参数也驱动自全局控制台，而不是保持独立——这样所有图表才能围绕同一组参数协调变化。

在合成部分，我想展示ATM Greeks随时间的演变（用对数或线性时间轴），验证Gamma与1/√T成正比、Vega与√T成正比的关系。还要加一个Gamma-Theta镜像叠加，以及在悬停位置实时分解PDE——特别是在ATM点用实际数字验证Θ + ½σ²S²Γ + rSΔ − rV ≈ 0这个恒等式，这需要年化Theta（日Theta乘以365）。同时确认Put的Theta公式，并在Delta图表底部添加y轴标签。

现在转向SVG图表引擎的实现细节：基于viewBox的响应式设计，带边距和虚线网格（低透明度），从数据点生成路径，近期曲线用虚线样式，图例放在标题下方作为紧凑的行布局。悬停交互通过透明矩形捕捉鼠标移动，找到最近的S值，显示垂直线、曲线上的点和工具提示框，所有图表通过共享事件总线同步。

坐标轴刻度约6-8个，格式化显示。

添加播放按钮动画，将timeNear从当前值在6秒内缓动到0.5，使用requestAnimationFrame更新图表（仅近期曲线和合成部分变化），滑块也随之更新，性能上每帧重算200个点乘以几条曲线完全可行。还考虑在悬停时显示市场状态摘要，包括Greeks和隐含波动率，但更简洁的方案是在控制台显示当前十字线位置的所有值。

改用在每个图表的tooltip中嵌入mini readouts，配合同步十字线。响应式设计让图表全宽显示，移动端堆叠排列。

配色方案采用品牌色：远期曲线用深青色，近期用赤陶色虚线，IV曲线用紫色，参考ATM线用墨色点线。卡片背景用浅羊皮纸色，边框用棕色。

文字用深墨色。

字体选择Noto Serif SC作为主字体，数值部分用系统等宽字体。页面结构包括顶部标题"期权希腊字母·统一图谱"及副标题说明数据来源，下方是粘性控制台显示K/S₀、r、σ、T近、T远等参数。

接下来是导语段落、五张图表卡片（分别展示Δ、Γ、Θ、ν、IV），每张卡片包含公式、SVG可视化、结论和原图对照。最后是整合视角部分，包含ATM期限结构图表和Gamma-Theta镜像分析。

整个文件会是一个相当规模的HTML文档，我需要分块构建来确保质量。

我会先创建基础框架和样式，然后逐步追加JavaScript引擎和内容初始化。在开始编码前，我应该快速查阅前端设计指南，虽然用户的设计系统（羊皮纸色、青绿色、陶土色和思源宋体）会优先应用，但还是要遵循环境的最佳实践。

现在我需要验证数学实现——用Python对照scipy的结果来检查几个关键值，确保JavaScript中的正态分布计算是准确的。我会用Abramowitz和Stegun的误差函数近似来实现normCDF，然后在Node中运行相同的公式进行对比验证。

接下来规划图表的具体参数：Delta图表的标的价格范围从0.5K到1.5K，纵轴从−1.05到1.05，加上水平参考线（0为实线，±0.5为灰色虚线）和标签标注关键点的期权状态。Gamma、Theta和Vega图表的标的范围是0.7K到1.3K。IV图表则按执行价格范围0.75S到1.25S绘制，标签方向相反。

现在计算Gamma在不同时间框架下的具体数值：近期30天时ATM的Gamma约为0.0461，而远期365天时约为0.01264，峰值比约3.6倍。动画过渡到0.5天时Gamma会显著上升到约0.359，展示时间衰减对Gamma的影响。

关键问题是动画过程中如何处理Y轴缩放——每帧动态调整会削弱"爆炸"效果，但固定到极值也有其优势。我倾向于每帧自动缩放，让近期曲线急剧上升时轴线随之扩展，同时远期曲线相对压低，这样能更直观地展现两条曲线的对比。

我会在gamma卡片上添加实时的峰值倍数标注，显示近期和远期ATM gamma的比值。

对于theta，我在计算近期ATM日theta时遇到了一些数值——正在验证第一项的计算（涉及标准差、时间衰减等参数），然后处理第二项中的正态分布部分。

远期的theta计算显示出明显的差异，近期约为−0.0638/天，远期约为−0.0222/天。

现在看vega的数据：近期ATM vega约0.1138，远期约0.379，远期是近期的3.3倍——这与gamma的模式相反。我还在检查波动率微笑在价格边界处的影响，看起来在±25的货币性处会产生显著的波动率变化。

根据图表，K=75时IV约86%，在K≈103.6处达到最小值约29%，然后在K=125处上升到约61%，这是一条非常陡峭的微笑曲线，与原始图像的渲染完全一致。

现在我要合成ATM期限结构，从1天到365天计算Gamma、Vega和每日Theta，每个都按其范围内的最大值归一化并绘制在0到1之间，标注Gamma和Theta与1/√T成正比，而Vega与√T成正比的关系。我还要绘制Gamma-Theta镜像叠加图，显示每日Theta和半方差项如何在短期内几乎重合，其间隙代表融资项。

现在添加图例来解释这个可视化，然后创建一个PDE验证卡片，在ATM处显示实时数据，验证Theta加上Gamma项加上Delta项减去价值项等于零，残差约为1e-12，并列出每一项的具体数值。最后添加一个对应表，映射原始文件到各个部分，说明原始参数和所做的更改，比如从静态PNG转换为交互式SVG，从多个工作簿合并为单一参数状态，以及配色方案的调整。

我会用中文标注坐标轴和图例，保留希腊字母和公式，标题定为「希腊字母统一图谱 · Greeks Unified Atlas」，副标题强调五个Greeks作为d1的投影。整个页面结构包括头部、粘性控制台、主内容区域，其中各个Greek分别占据独立的卡片部分，最后是综合部分展示期限结构和PDE验证。

现在设计脚本架构：建立一个通用的Chart类，接收配置对象（包括定义域函数、数据序列生成函数、坐标轴刻度、参考线、标签和格式化方法），每次状态更新时重新计算数据点、构建比例尺、生成SVG字符串并绑定悬停交互。通过中央事件总线同步所有图表的悬停状态，用滑块控制K、r、σ、期限等参数，并在动画循环中持续更新。

Building the interactive framework... Decimal places vary by metric: IV uses percentage format. For the crosshair sync across charts, I'm handling different domains by syncing on absolute spot price S — clamping or hiding when S falls outside a chart's range. The IV chart shares the same strike axis around the spot price, so syncing makes sense there; I'll label it with the strike price. The mirror chart syncs too, but the term-structure chart (time on x-axis) stays independent. For tooltips, I'm using a small pinned readout box in the top-right of each card rather than a floating global tooltip, which avoids jitter and keeps the display cleaner.

For animation, I'm stretching time near expiry by animating in square-root time space instead of linear days — this gives more animation frames where the action happens. During the animation, the time slider gets disabled and shows a live countdown display.

The synthesis chart animates along with the time parameter, while the term structure chart stays static but displays moving markers at the current near and far tenor positions. I'm also handling edge cases where near tenor exceeds far tenor (still valid, just labeled with day counts), and setting reasonable bounds on all inputs: time from 1–365 days, far tenor 30–730, strike 50–200, volatility 5–100%, and rates 0–10%.

For the delta chart at short expiry, I need enough resolution to capture the step around the strike — using 400 points across the range gives smooth curves even when the transition width is only a few points wide. The far-tenor deltas will use the same colors as near-tenor but at 70% opacity to distinguish them, with the legend showing all four curves: far call, near call, far put, near put.

Now checking the theta calculation for a deep ITM put at S=70, T=365 days: working through d1 and d2, the first term (gamma decay) is negative but the second term (interest rate benefit) turns positive and dominates, giving a net positive theta of about 0.0036 per day — a nice illustration of how deep ITM puts can have positive theta when rates are meaningful.

I'll also note the spreadsheet origin with a small footnote referencing the source file and the specific cells. Setting up the color palette now with the paper background, card surfaces, ink tones for text, and accent colors in teal, terra, and plum for the visual hierarchy.

I'm planning to write the file in chunks using a bash heredoc approach, being careful with template literals and backtick escaping. Before I start building though, I should review the frontend design guidelines first to make sure I'm following the right approach. Then I'll structure the Greeks section with a logical narrative flow — Delta leading into Gamma as its derivative, Theta as the time decay component, Vega for volatility sensitivity, and finally IV to acknowledge non-constant volatility — each building on the previous concept.

      "text": "     1	---
     2	name: frontend-design
     3	description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
     4	license: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt
     5	---
     6	
     7	# Frontend Design
     8	
     9	Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.
    10	
    11	## Ground it in the subject
    12	
    13	If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.
    14	
    15	## Design principles
    16	
    17	For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.
    18	
    19	Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.
    20	
    21	Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

sections.label: 推理过程
sections.text:
So the parchment, teal, and terracotta palette with Noto Serif SC isn't a generic AI cliché here—it's Chow's established personal brand that he's consistently applied across his work. The brief itself anchors the visual direction, and when the brief pins something down that clearly, I should follow it exactly rather than second-guess it as a design default.

The core signature move is a synchronized crosshair that sweeps across all five Greeks charts while the "T→0 到期演化" animation plays, letting delta, gamma, theta, and vega all respond to a single master time control. That's the memorable, grounded element that ties everything together.

I'm mapping out the full design system now: the color palette from parchment backgrounds through teal and terracotta accents, the typography mixing Noto Serif SC for display and body with monospace for numerics, and the layout structure with a sticky console strip, five chart cards flowing through the Greeks, an integration section with term structure and PDE checks, and a faithful reproduction table at the bottom.

Now I'm building the JavaScript engine to handle the math—implementing the normal distribution PDF and error function with proper numerical coefficients...

Implementing the cumulative normal distribution function and then calculating the Greeks: delta for calls and puts based on whether we're in or out of the money, plus gamma...

Now I'm computing theta on a daily basis by breaking it into components for calls versus puts, vega scaled to percentage changes, and the Black-Scholes call price formula. I'm also modeling implied volatility skew as a quadratic function of the strike relative to the spot price, then setting up the initial state with strike, rate, and volatility parameters.

I'm building a chart factory that takes configuration for axes labels, formatting, and domain/range calculations, then renders the visualization by computing data series, determining y-axis bounds, and drawing gridlines with axis labels.

Adding reference lines, zone labels, and the crosshair layer...

The charts sync hover interactions across a group—when the user moves the mouse, I compute the x-value from the inverted scale and broadcast it to all charts in the group, showing or hiding the crosshair depending on whether that x-value falls within each chart's domain. The readout row displays ATM values by default.

For animation, I'm building a play button that animates the time parameter in square-root space over 8 seconds, updating the slider and legend chips each frame, then showing a replay option when done. There's also a progress label showing remaining time, and the slider gets disabled during playback. The renderAll function refreshes all charts and the PDE card on each animation frame.

Now setting up the control sliders for strike ratio K, interest rate r, volatility σ, and the two time parameters tNear and tFar with their respective ranges and step sizes. For the term structure chart, I'm plotting normalized Greeks across a 365-day range with moving markers at the near and far months, and a second chart showing the same Greeks across different spot prices.

For the mirror chart, I'm decomposing theta into its daily decay component and the gamma-based funding term, using the call option formula to show how these two pieces contribute to total theta. I'll add a thin line to highlight the funding gap between them. Then on the PDE card, I'm computing the full theta breakdown at the strike price and near-term date, displaying each component—theta annualized, gamma funding, delta carry, and financing cost—in a live table.

Now I'm setting up the zone labels across the strike spectrum: at 0.75K, K, and 1.25K I'll mark whether calls and puts are in or out of the money, with the center zone labeled as ATM (平值). The IV chart will flip the ITM/OTM labels left and right to reflect the volatility smile. I'm rendering these as two-line SVG text elements, and adding vertical reference lines at the strike with a legend entry for the strike price.

For the y-axis formatting, I need to handle different precision levels depending on the metric—delta gets two decimal places, gamma uses 3–4 significant figures, theta shows four decimals, vega three decimals, and implied volatility displays as a percentage. I'm also implementing a nice-number tick generator to keep the axes clean.

Writing the prose content... 近月期权的 ATM Delta 实际上略高于 0.5，因为利率和波动率项把它推高了一点。Gamma 衡量的是期权凸性的密度分布，在 ATM 处达到峰值，Call 和 Put 的 Gamma 完全相同。由于 Gamma 与时间平方根成反比，临近到期时会急剧上升——30 天期的峰值约是 365 天期的 3.6 倍，而 0DTE 期权的 Gamma 甚至能达到 30 倍，这解释了做市商在到期日临近时需要大幅增加对冲频率的原因。

远离 ATM 时 Gamma 迅速衰减，深度 ITM 和 OTM 的期权都失去了期权性。Theta 本质上是 Gamma 的成本账单，两者的曲线形状互为镜像，这反映了无套利的会计恒等式：持有凸性必须按日支付租金，近月 ATM 期权的 Theta 衰减最快。

对于 Put 期权，深度 ITM 时 Theta 可能为正，因为等待行权能获得利息补贴。Vega 与 Gamma 形状相似但时间维度相反，远月期权才是波动率敏感性的主要载体，365 天期权的 Vega 是 30 天期权的三倍多。

这种时间不对称性是日历价差交易的核心逻辑：卖近月获取 Theta 和 Gamma，买远月获取 Vega，而做空 0DTE 期权时几乎没有卖出任何波动率敞口。现在考虑隐含波动率不是常数的情况，用行权价作横轴来观察波动率微笑曲线，这反映了市场对不同行权价的真实波动率预期。

股票期权的典型曲线呈现"微笑加左偏"的形状，其中抛物线部分代表两翼的微笑，而线性负项把低行权价一侧推得更高——这是市场对崩盘风险的永久定价，1987 年之后留下的疤痕。曲线的最低点不在平值而是偏向 OTM Call 一侧，这意味着 BSM 模型在每个行权价都需要用不同的波动率，模型本身虽然错误，但这种错误的规律性本身就成了可交易的对象。

现在我在思考如何把五个工作簿、五段宏和五张图表整合成一个统一的系统，让它们共享同一组参数和时间轴——拖动任何滑杆时所有图表同步更新，按下到期演化按钮时能在同一时刻看到 Delta、Gamma、Theta、Vega 的全部变化。原有的视觉语言都保留下来：近月和远月的对比、ATM 参考线、Call/Put 的双视角标注，以及默认参数设置。

在期限结构这一部分，我发现了一个关键的对称性：在同一个 ATM 点上，Gamma 与时间的平方根成反比，而 Vega 与时间的平方根成正比——短期是 Gamma 的主导，长期被 Vega 统治。把三条曲线都归一化后放在一起，Theta 和 Gamma 几乎完全重叠（因为 Theta 的主要成分就是负的时间衰减项），而 Vega 单调反向。两个标记点会跟随控制台中近月和远月的选择移动。

对于镜像验证部分，我在同一坐标系上画出负 Theta 和半倍 Sigma 平方乘以 S 平方乘以 Gamma 除以 365，两条线几乎完全重合，只有微小的缝隙来自资金成本项——这不是拟合而是恒等式的直接可视化，展示你每天实际付出的时间价值。

现在验证 PDE 台账，对 ATM 和近月的看涨期权进行实时数值检验，残差达到浮点噪音级别。还要补充表格说明和公式行，以及生成信息的脚注。最后整理控制台的输入参数标签。

现在添加近月和远月的剩余天数显示，以及动画播放和复位按钮，动画运行时按钮切换为停止状态并显示剩余天数。Theta 卡片支持看涨和看跌的切换，波动率滑块与 IV 图表联动，悬停时显示垂直参考线和数据点，工具提示固定在图表上方显示数据行，并标注货币性百分比。还要处理期限结构和镜像图表。

镜像图表加入现货同步组，期限图表独立显示三个标准化值和原始值，K 滑块改变时重新计算定义域范围，IV 图的 S₀ 始终等于 K。调整 delta 区域标签的垂直对齐，每条曲线采用 320 个数据点，为各坐标轴添加标题，图例文本动态更新以显示期限和期权类型。

现在规划 ATM 读数卡片的默认显示内容：delta 卡显示近月和远月的 delta 差值，gamma 卡显示 gamma 值及倍数，theta、vega 和 IV 卡各自显示对应的近远月数据。

Building the card structure... Writing component styles... Writing CSS tokens... Writing component styles... Writing animation logic... Both chart groups render and redraw their crosshairs when the bus has a value. I'm structuring each chart as an object with svg, root element, legend element, config, scales, series points, and methods for updating, drawing crosshairs, and setting readouts. For the terminal chart, hovering shows values at that time point in raw units plus the markers legend, and since the mirror chart is part of the spot group, they sync together. Different domains across charts (delta 0.5–1.5K versus gamma 0.7–1.3) mean when hovering outside a chart's range, it hides the crosshair and reverts to the ATM default rather than clamping to an edge.

The IV chart uses strike price as its x-axis, syncing the same numeric position across charts even though the interpretation differs—this vertical alignment actually reveals the strike versus spot symmetry nicely. I'm adding it to the spot group with readout labels showing the strike price, plus a moneyness percentage chip calculated as (S/K−1)×100 to display like "+5.0%". Now I'm laying out the formula chips for the Greeks: delta as N(d₁) for calls and N(d₁)−1 for puts, gamma as φ(d₁)/(Sσ√T), and theta with its longer expression that I'll need to format compactly.

Writing HTML structure... Implementing the Black-Scholes pricing functions... Finishing the vega calculation, then setting up the call option pricing formula and an implied volatility skew function. Now I'm initializing the global state with default parameters for the Black-Scholes model—strike price, risk-free rate, volatility, and time horizons—along with utility functions for DOM access and number formatting.

I'm also creating a helper to generate evenly-spaced values across a range, and implementing a function that calculates nice tick marks for chart axes by determining an appropriate step size based on the data span.

Now I'm setting up the core SVG chart engine with dimensions and margins, initializing a chart object that will manage the SVG element, render target, legend, and scale functions.

Writing chart update logic... Writing SVG grid and tick marks... Writing SVG paths... Writing SVG legend and interaction handlers... Adding pointer event handlers... Writing event handlers and utility functions... Writing chart configuration... Completing the series data with put option curves for both near and far expiration dates, then adding reference lines for the strike price and horizontal levels, and finally defining zones to label the moneyness regions across the chart. Writing component readout... Zones go at the bottom for consistency. The legend shows near/far month labels plus the strike price chip. Theta uses zero baseline with references at the current value and zero, formats to 3 decimals, and displays near/far readouts with 4 decimals and type labels—toggle buttons switch between theta types. Vega follows a similar pattern to gamma with 2 decimal formatting since values stay in the 0–0.4 range, and peaks scale with strike price. IV groups by spot price with the domain spanning 0.75K to 1.25K and labels the x-axis as strike price.

For the crosshair sync, I'm grouping delta, gamma, theta, vega, IV, and mirror together so they share hover updates, while the term chart operates independently. The global domain for clamping hover strikes is [0.5K, 1.5K], which covers the widest range across all charts. Zone labels in delta sit at the bottom of the plot area, and the term chart domain extends from 1 to the maximum of 365 or the far expiration date.

On the term chart, I'm placing vertical dashed reference lines at the near and far expiration dates with Chinese labels. For the mirror chart, I'm showing the negative theta decay as a solid line and the gamma convexity rent as a dashed line, with the readout displaying both components plus a gap for the funding term. The PDE breakdown table lists out each component—time decay, convexity rent, delta funding benefit, and option funding cost—with their respective values.

I'm adding a header row inside the table that displays the current parameter context (spot, strike, time, volatility, delta, gamma), then the four term rows plus the residual sum. For the animation, I'm using a square-root space interpolation over 8 seconds down to 0.5 days, with the button toggling playback and the slider disabled during animation. Once it finishes, the button switches to a replay icon, and clicking it restores the saved time if the current value is still above 0.6 days. During animation, the time badge shows one decimal place.

For the slider behavior, I'm setting the minimum to 1 day, but when the animation programmatically sets the value to 0.5 days, the HTML range input clamps it to the minimum—so the thumb stays pinned at the left while the badge displays the true value, which is fine. The slider's input listener won't interfere since it's disabled during animation. On reset, I'm clearing the animation state, re-enabling the slider, restoring the button to its play state, and resetting the theta type back to 'call' with the segment buttons updated accordingly.

For rendering, I'm updating all charts, recalculating the PDE, and syncing the badge values. With gamma formatting, I need to handle the edge case where very small volatility and large strike values produce tiny gamma values—toFixed(3) should work fine for the typical range of ticks, though I'm double-checking the scale calculations to ensure no values round to zero unexpectedly.

I'm implementing an adaptive formatting function that picks the right number of decimal places based on the magnitude of each value, so gamma, theta, vega, and mirror y-axis ticks all display cleanly without unnecessary precision or rounding artifacts. Delta will stay fixed at one decimal place.

For the Greeks and IV displays, I'm handling delta ticks from −1.0 to 1.0 with one decimal, IV percentages formatted as whole numbers with a percent sign, and theta ticks (which are often small negatives) using the same adaptive formatter. Strike prices on the x-axis will round to integers, and the term structure chart will use days as the x-axis unit.

I'm positioning the zones at different moneyness levels—delta uses 0.75K, K, and 1.25K, while the others use 0.85K, K, and 1.15K—with IV zones also at 0.85 and 1.15 of the spot price but with flipped labels. Each chart gets its own legend array, and the K chip label pulls from live state. The readout for theta includes the option type (Call or Put), and for IV I'm showing the hovered strike's implied volatility, the ATM volatility, the valley point where the smile reaches its minimum, and that minimum IV value itself.

For the mirror readout, I'm decomposing theta into its funding cost component—the rent from gamma hedging—and the funding cost of carrying the strike, then displaying the gap between negative theta and rent as the funding term. The term chart readout shows gamma, vega, and theta raw values at the money, computed at the current time to expiration. For the series colors, gamma is terra solid, vega is teal solid, and absolute theta is gold with a thin dashed line.

**整合层**——原版看不见的三样东西：陆·一节的 **ATM期限结构图**（Γ∝1/√T与ν∝√T背向而行，近/远标记线跟随滑杆）；**Γ–Θ镜像验证图**（−Θ与½σ²S²Γ/365几乎重合，缝隙即资金项，把r拉到0缝隙闭合）；**PDE实时台账**（四项之和残差10⁻¹⁵——验证时发现N(x)近似误差在恒等式各项间代数对消，这点写进了正文）。

**交互层**——跨图同步金色十字光标（悬停任一图，其余同步显示精确读数）；**「到期演化」动画**把T近从当前值按√T节奏压至0.5天，Delta数字化、Gamma爆炸至28倍、Theta见底、Vega流干同屏发生；Theta卡激活了原脚本存而未用的Put分支（可看到深度ITM Put的正Theta，S=70时+0.0036/天）。

一个可以立刻试的动作：打开后直接按「▷ 到期演化」，然后把σ滑杆拉高重播——0DTE的物理学一目了然。

sections.text:
I'm creating a long call payoff diagram showing the profit/loss at expiration, with the strike at 100 and a 5-point premium, plotting the payoff across a stock price range from 80 to 120 with a green line for P/L, currency formatting on both axes, and reference lines for the zero point, strike price, and maximum loss.

Now I'm adding the breakeven point at 105 with an arrow, labeling the regions as out-of-the-money on the left and in-the-money on the right, noting unlimited max profit at the top right, and placing a legend in the lower right corner.

The user wants this converted into a web program integrated into their design system. The key insight is that a static expiration payoff diagram only shows the final hockey-stick shape, but the real depth comes from showing how the option's value evolves over time—the Black-Scholes curve that sits above the payoff line and gradually collapses onto it as expiration approaches, revealing the time value component that's invisible in a static diagram.

This connects directly to the Greeks work from before: the gap between the BSM curve and the kinked payoff is where Theta decay and Gamma convexity live. I should also add a time slider to show how the breakeven point shifts from near the current spot price toward K+premium as expiration approaches, since retail traders often misread the static breakeven annotation. The app can display the long call's Greek profile as live readouts, and potentially add a probability lens showing the market-implied chance of profit under lognormal assumptions.

For the visual design, I'm thinking about how to map the color palette from the previous atlas work—teal for the structural expiration payoff line and terracotta for the pre-expiration MTM curve to reflect the time-decay urgency semantics, though there's a tension since expiration is technically the shortest time horizon. Actually, I should honor the original's green payoff line by using teal instead—it's in the same color family and fits the parchment palette while maintaining semantic continuity. The MTM curve becomes terracotta (time-burning), but I need to differentiate the max loss line so it doesn't collide with the MTM curve, both being terracotta.

I'm settling on gold for the pre-expiration MTM curve—it captures the metaphor of time value melting away, and the translucent gold shading between the MTM and payoff lines creates a beautiful visual of that eroding time premium against the parchment background.

For the breakeven points, I'll mark the accounting breakeven as a solid ink dot with an annotation, and then add a second moving breakeven on the gold MTM curve itself to show where the real P&L crosses zero before expiration.

Now I'm thinking through the feature set: the faithful layer needs the hockey stick payoff, axes in currency, the max loss line, both breakeven markers, the region labels, and the unlimited profit annotation. For the console inputs, I need to handle the premium carefully—in faithful mode it's a free parameter, but when I add the BSM layer, the premium should automatically equal the theoretical price at entry based on the spot, volatility, rate, and time to expiration.

I'll keep the interface simple by letting the user input the strike and premium directly (like the original), then add sliders for volatility, interest rate, and remaining time to expiration so the MTM curve updates dynamically. The MTM value is just the BSM price minus the premium paid, and at expiration it converges to the payoff. I could add a hint showing what premium the model would suggest for an ATM entry at the original entry time, which gives context without forcing the user into a specific mode.

For the time dimension, I'm adding a slider that scrubs from the initial time down to zero, and as it moves the MTM curve animates down onto the intrinsic value payoff—that "time decay melting" effect is the core visual. Then below that I'll show a live dashboard that displays the Greeks, time value, intrinsic value, and P/L at whatever spot price the user hovers over or at ATM by default.

I'm also adding a shaded band between the two curves to highlight the time value component, and I want to include some interpretive sections that break down the payoff structure—explaining the max loss equals premium paid, the breakeven point, and the asymmetric risk profile. In the risk-neutral framework, that drift difference between μ and r shifts the probability landscape. Now I'm thinking about how to structure the visualization: a unified main chart that layers both the payoff skeleton and the time-value curve together with the gold shading, showing them as an integrated whole rather than separate pieces. Then I'll add sections for the time decay animation, displaying how the MTM curves evolve across different time points as expiration approaches.

I'm also planning to highlight the break-even trajectory—where MTM equals zero as a function of remaining time—which traces from near the entry price toward the strike plus premium. That's the core insight most retail traders miss. Finally, I'll map out the position Greeks against spot price at the current time point.

For the probability perspective, I want to overlay a lognormal distribution of the terminal stock price with the payoff regions shaded: total loss below the strike, partial loss between strike and break-even, and profit above break-even. The chart shows the density curve with these three zones marked and their corresponding probabilities calculated from the normal distribution—this reveals how the hockey-stick payoff gets weighted by actual likelihood, which typically results in an expected P/L near zero.

Then I'll add a note on the risk-neutral perspective: if you buy at fair value, the discounted expected profit is exactly zero, which means you're not paying for expected returns but for the shape of the distribution itself. I'll also include a section documenting how to replicate these calculations, plus interactive console parameters for strike, premium, volatility, rate, and time to expiration.

For the remaining time slider, I'm setting it to range from 0 to 365 days with a default of 60, animating the decay as time approaches zero. The spot price domain stays faithful to the original at 0.8K to 1.2K, and I'm positioning the payoff labels at the bottom inside the chart like before, with the max profit annotation clearly marked.

Now I need to add the breakeven annotation with an arrow pointing to the breakeven spot, and then tackle the probability density chart — which requires deciding on an initial spot price S₀ parameter since the density depends on where we start, unlike the MTM curve which just shows current value across different spot prices.

The probability card will update with the hovered spot price, showing the odds of profit and total loss at expiration. I'll use the strike as the default S₀ but let it sync with the crosshair. For the density visualization, I'm drawing a lognormal distribution of the terminal stock price, shading three regions: below strike in terracotta for total loss, between strike and breakeven in gold for partial recovery, and above breakeven in teal for profit, with vertical lines marking the strike and breakeven levels and labels showing the probability of each outcome.

Implementing the lognormal probability density function... For the breakeven strike calculation, I need to search across a wider range—from 0.2K to 3K—since the call value grows monotonically and will eventually exceed any reasonable premium. I'm also planning the visualization layout: a trajectory chart showing how the breakeven strike evolves over time from 0 to 365 days, with the y-axis spanning from K to K plus the premium, and a marker indicating the current slider position. This would sit alongside the ghost family chart and probability density plot, creating a multi-panel dashboard.

For the ghost family curves, I'm interpolating between different time fractions of the current slider value—at 100%, 75%, 50%, 25%, and 10% of T—with colors transitioning from gold to teal, and small labels at the right edge showing the time values. The family should respond dynamically to the slider, though I need to guard against degenerate cases when T approaches zero. I'm also adding a fair value hint that calculates the ATM call premium using Black-Scholes at the current time, displayed as a chip in the console.

The dashboard will show intrinsic value, time value, mark-to-market P/L, the Greeks (delta, gamma, theta per day, vega), breakeven at expiration and the true breakeven for the current time, with identity chips summarizing the directional sensitivities. Hovering over the main chart syncs the dashboard display, and I'm setting up crosshair synchronization across the first three charts while keeping the breakeven-vs-time chart on its own hover group.

For the time decay animation, I'm collapsing the MTM curve onto the payoff diagram as T approaches zero, shrinking the gold shading area and sliding the true breakeven marker toward the strike plus premium. The probability density chart will clamp its time axis at a minimum of one day to prevent it from becoming unreadably narrow, with a label indicating when that clamping is active.

The opening prose emphasizes that the payoff diagram only captures the T=0 moment, while actual positions exist across the entire T>0 interval.

Now I'm building out the core structure: the payoff line has just three degrees of freedom—the floor at negative premium, the kink at strike, and the 45° upslope—but each one encodes a contract term. I'm keeping the parameters from before (K=100, premium=5) and inheriting the volatility and rate assumptions (σ=30%, r=5%) to maintain consistency with the Greeks chart.

The floor represents the buyer's maximum loss (the full premium paid upfront), the kink is where optionality concentrates (all the Gamma mass from the earlier framework), and the slope becomes delta=1 in the post-expiration region. I'm clarifying why the breakeven point at K+premium ($105) is misleading before expiration—the golden BSM curve sits above the payoff line, and that vertical gap is time value, which Theta drains daily in exchange for the convexity Gamma provides.

Now I'm examining how time value decays unevenly across the strike spectrum: it's thickest at-the-money and melts fastest there, while the deep wings have almost nothing to decay—this is just another way to visualize the Theta valley from the earlier framework. With five time slices (T, ¾T, ½T, ¼T, 0.1T) plus the expiration skeleton, I can see the entire decay pattern at once. I'm verifying the deep ITM behavior: the time value there equals K(1−e^{−rT}), which stays positive even as intrinsic value dominates, confirming European calls always retain some time value until expiration.

The break-even point itself migrates upward as time passes—the longer you hold, the higher the stock needs to climb to offset theta decay. This migration path is how theta's cost manifests visually. When time is abundant, break-even can sit below your entry price if the underlying barely moves or IV rises; but as expiration approaches, break-even converges toward strike plus premium paid.

I'm also noting how break-even responds to volatility shifts—adjusting the IV slider reveals this sensitivity immediately. Then there's the probability lens: when you buy at fair value, the risk-neutral expected profit is zero, so what you're really purchasing is the shape of the distribution itself—trading a defined small loss for unlimited upside exposure. The density chart overlays probabilities across the payoff curve's three regions: total loss below strike, partial recovery in the middle, and profit above break-even.

With standard parameters (spot equals strike, 60 days to expiration, 30% volatility), I'm calculating the exact probabilities—roughly 35% chance of profit at break-even, nearly 50% chance of total loss, and about 16% in the partial recovery zone. The expected value still zeros out despite these asymmetric odds.

The key insight is that risk-neutral pricing uses the risk-free rate rather than the true drift, so the real probability of profit depends entirely on your private forecast of the underlying's actual return—that's the entire reason to buy the call in the first place. I'm also noting the structure for the writeup: preserving the original table format and currency styling while adding the BSM fair value hint, with headers in both English and Chinese covering the long call strategy and payoff anatomy.

Now I'm setting up the interactive visualization framework with the payoff kernel max(S−K,0) displayed as (S−K)⁺, along with input controls for strike, premium, volatility, rate, and time to expiration (defaulting to 60 days out of 365), plus a fair value chip and a time decay slider that animates T toward zero with a reset button. The axes will format prices as dollar amounts with appropriate decimal precision.

Building the chart layers... Adding SVG annotations... I'll add a watchHover config flag so the probability chart updates whenever the main hover changes, and give the density chart its own local crosshair that shows the tail probability at the hovered S_T value rather than syncing to the global S0 hover.

For the BE* trajectory chart, I'm computing the Bellman equation values across the 365-day range using bisection (120 points, ~40 iterations each per render, which stays cheap even during animation), then adding independent hover to read out the BE* value at any hovered day. The ghost family shows historical trajectories at fractional time points [1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1] scaled to the current state time, with gold colors at decreasing opacity and thinner lines except the first one; if the current time is under 2 days I'll collapse to a single ghost with a note.

For the dashboard card, I'm laying out a grid of stat tiles showing the current spot price, option value, intrinsic and time value, P&L, Greeks (delta, gamma, theta per day, vega), expiration BE, current BE*, and probability of profit at expiration—roughly 12 tiles in a 4-column grid with a risk-neutral note. The legend updates dynamically based on the time slider, and at the animation end I'm showing a message that time value has decayed to zero.

At exactly T=0, the MTM curve should collapse to the payoff curve, so I'm guarding against division by zero in the Black-Scholes calculation (when σ√T becomes zero) by checking if T is near zero and returning intrinsic value directly. Similar guards exist for delta, gamma, theta, and vega at expiration. The time slider now allows T to reach exactly 0, and the animation will linearly decay the days to zero. At T=0, the breakeven point is simply strike plus premium.

For the density view near T=0, I'm clamping the effective time to at least 1 day to avoid numerical issues. The fair value chip will show the intrinsic value when T=0, which might be zero at-the-money, and the label will indicate the current time remaining. The default time horizon is 60 days since the original visualization had no time dimension, and I'm adding this slider as a new feature. I'll reuse and extend the CSS styling from the previous implementation.

Now I'm planning the build structure—around 750 lines across three sections—then running the same verification pipeline: syntax checking, mathematical validation against scipy benchmarks for call values and probabilities, DOM interaction testing, and visual verification of the main payoff, density, and trajectory charts. I'm naming the file "买入看涨损益解剖.html" to match the Chinese branding. Let me compute the scipy reference values for the default parameters and verify the deep in-the-money behavior.

I'm extending the JavaScript engine with configuration options for rendering filled polygon areas before the series, appending raw SVG elements after for annotations and markers, and setting up hover-triggered re-renders for charts whose series depend on hover state, with the dashboard update integrated into the broadcast system.

Now laying out the three main charts: the payoff diagram showing intrinsic value and mark-to-market curves with zones, reference lines, and annotations for breakeven points and max profit; the time decay melt chart with opacity-graded curves across different time horizons; and the breakeven trajectory chart tracking how the breakeven price evolves over the calendar year.

For the probability distribution chart, I'm setting up the domain to span from 80% to 120% of strike, with the effective time calculated carefully to avoid edge cases. The chart will show the probability density function as a plum-colored line with three shaded regions underneath representing different outcome zones, plus vertical reference lines at the strike and the breakeven price, and a readout displaying the probabilities for each region.

On hover, I'm adding a crosshair that calculates the tail probability to the right of the cursor position. For the dashboard, I'm building a set of tiles that update based on the current spot price from the hover position or the strike as default—showing the spot price, option value, intrinsic value, time value, position P&L with conditional styling, delta, and gamma.

I'm also adding tiles for theta per day, vega, break-even at expiration, the real break-even accounting for premium paid, and the probability of profit at expiration—twelve tiles total. The fair value tile displays the at-the-money option price for a 60-day horizon, and clicking it sets the premium to that fair value while clamping it to the slider range and syncing everything. For the real break-even solver, I'm implementing a binary search that finds where the option value equals the premium paid, handling edge cases where time to expiration is negligible.

I'm also refining the currency formatting to handle negative values more naturally, showing a minus sign before the dollar symbol rather than after. Adding breakeven annotation... 对原版的解读：longcall.py 画的是教科书曲棍球棍——P/L = max(0,S−K) − 权利金，B1:B2 = {K=100, $5}，带最大亏损线、盈亏平衡箭头、OTM/ATM/ITM 分区、"Max Profit: Unlimited"。要素全部逐一复刻（绿→深青、红→赤陶，沿用上一份的翻译规则），$ 货币坐标保留。

I'm noticing a discrepancy in the data export — the 期权数据 sheet shows all zeros for open interest because the write operation only captured the first thousand rows, yet the 痛点分析 sheet contains actual nonzero loss values with a minimum of 250 and total of 289,325, suggesting the live-fetched OI values were used in the calculations but didn't make it into the final data dump.

Looking at the timestamps and status indicators, it seems like the data sheet comes from an interrupted run (control B5 frozen mid-fetch, B2 showing 2025-10-10) while the pain analysis table retained results from a successful earlier run dated 2025-10-17 with 73 strikes. So the real dataset I should work with is the 痛点分析 table itself, and I can actually recover the per-strike open interest values by treating the loss curves as an inverse problem — since call loss is piecewise linear in price with slope changes at each strike, I can extract the open interest from the second differences of the loss function.

Now I'm working through the math: the forward slope of call loss between consecutive strikes gives me the cumulative call OI up to that point, so the difference between consecutive slopes yields the individual strike OI. I'm applying the same logic backwards for puts, using the slope of put loss to extract cumulative put OI from above, then differencing to get per-strike values.

Once I verify this inversion works—recomputing the pain curve from the recovered OI matches the original cached data—I'll have both the strike ladder and a validated methodology. Then I can build the web app as a max pain calculator and visualizer, though it'll need to work around the limitation that a web version can't directly call the Futu API like the original pipeline does.

The app itself will replicate the exact algorithm in JavaScript with the same double-loop logic and loss-minimization semantics, embed the real GOOGL 2025-10-17 data (73 strikes with recovered OI) as a default dataset anchored to the cached max pain of $250, and provide an input layer where users can paste in their own strike chains from any broker or generate synthetic ones with lognormal OI clustering around a chosen spot price. The visualization component is the key addition—the original only printed results, so I'll build something that actually shows the pain curve and lets users explore different scenarios. I'm weighing whether to add sensitivity analysis showing how much max pain shifts per 10k OI at each strike, but that might be overkill. Better to keep it focused: the pain curve itself with call and put components on a linear scale to show that dramatic V-shape, plus the mirrored OI bars with the max pain overlay.

For the cash flow breakdown at the pin, I need to account for the 100× lot size multiplier that converts the per-share losses into actual dollar amounts. Then as the interactive piece, I'll build a what-if tool where users can inject OI at a chosen strike and watch the max pain shift in real time with before/after curve overlays—that's where the mechanism really clicks. After that comes the data input section for CSV paste or generation. Now I'm connecting this back to the trilogy structure — the field-level view, individual leg positions, and finally the aggregate market structure. For the algorithm transparency, I'm formulating the total pain calculation as a double sum across calls and puts evaluated on the strike grid, and noting that since the piecewise-linear loss function is convex, its minimum must occur at a strike rather than between them.

I'm also planning to embed a regression anchor using the GOOGL data — recomputing the cached pain analysis to verify it matches exactly, with a note about the verification residual being zero. Then I'll outline how the console takes the current price as input to drive the distance and magnetic attraction readouts.

For the interface layout, I'm thinking the data input (spot price, multiplier, dataset selection) goes in one card, while the console keeps the current price slider and contract multiplier toggle, with the what-if scenario controls in another section. I'll sync the hover states between the pain chart and the Greeks chart on the same strike axis, and let users inject what-if scenarios by toggling call/put, selecting a strike (either via dropdown or by clicking bars directly), and adjusting the open interest delta with a slider.

For the spot price default, I need to set it around $245 based on GOOGL's October 2025 trading range, with a note that it's adjustable since the cache doesn't include live pricing — I'll make it a slider spanning 150–350. On the main pain chart, the x-axis shows settlement prices across the full strike grid (70–350), but the interesting volatility structure lives in the 200–300 range, so I should consider defaulting the zoom to that central region while keeping the full range accessible. I'll focus the domain to where there's actual trading activity—strikes with open interest—and add a toggle for full view versus zoomed valley region. The main chart will show call and put open interest as separate lines in teal and terra with a thick gold line for total, plus the max pain and spot price markers. The second chart uses mirrored bars (calls up, puts down) to visualize the open interest distribution across strikes, synced to the same domain, and the what-if tool will let me click a strike to highlight it and overlay a projected curve on the main chart.

For the data input, I'm building a textarea that accepts flexible formats—comma, tab, or space-separated—with auto-detection and error handling. There's a synthetic generator with sliders for spot price, volatility skew, and a button to create sample data, plus a restore button for the original dataset. When data is applied, everything recalculates: domain resets, spot defaults to the midpoint, all charts re-render, and the data source chip updates to show how many custom strikes were loaded.

The display toggles between per-share contracts (default) and notional dollars scaled by 100, with thousand-separator formatting throughout. I'm also adding prose sections that explain the conceptual journey—from Greeks surfaces to individual positions to now mapping the entire market's open interest landscape at expiration—and noting how the original real-time pipeline from market data has been decomposed into portable pieces: the algorithm itself, cached historical data with OI ladders reverse-engineered from the pain points, and a universal paste interface replacing the live gateway connection.

Now I'm clarifying the definition of maximum holder loss as the minimum total intrinsic value (what sellers pay out least), then moving into the open interest terrain with call and put walls, the mechanical intuition of pin dynamics where sellers face bidirectional squeeze pressure, and finally the magnetic pull experiment—calculating how much OI at a single strike is needed to move the pin, with leverage peaking near the valley floor where the convex function flattens.

I'm also contrasting this with GEX as a framework: max pain represents intrinsic value statics while GEX captures hedging flow dynamics; both often converge at monthly OPEX but through different mechanisms. The academic foundation comes from Ni–Pearson–Poteshman (2005), which documented price clustering at strikes on expiration and attributed it to market maker hedging and partial manipulation, though the effect has weakened over two decades as market structure evolved. I'll integrate the limitations and counterexamples—particularly how 0DTE trading dilutes the relevance of OI—into the prose sections rather than separate charts, keeping the structure as dense narrative with a boundary-and-critique card and a data card at the end.

Now I'm organizing the layout: pain curve visualization, OI terrain with interactive selection, magnetic attraction experiment linked to the earlier sections, a text-only critique card covering scope and evidence, and a data entry point. I should also note the supporting scripts in the provenance—check_dates.py for listing AAPL expiries and run_max_pain.bat as the launcher.

For the algorithm itself, I'm preserving the core details: evaluation points are defined by the exact strike set via convexity, and when OI is missing the parser falls back to volume with a zero default. The parser accepts three to five columns (strike, call OI, put OI, optionally call volume and put volume) and applies the fallback rule consistently.

On tie-breaking, I'm keeping the first occurrence when strikes are equal—the minimum index scan preserves that. Units are per-share with a toggle for lot-size scaling. Now I'm working through the inversion math in Python: given sorted strikes and cumulative call/put spreads, I compute the implied OI at each strike by taking differences of the cumulative slopes, with the highest strike call OI set to zero since it's not identifiable from the grid. Embedding the recovered data as a compact JavaScript array with strike, call OI, and put OI values, then displaying key metrics on the dashboard like total call OI, total put OI, put-call ratio, pain points, and distance from current price. For the synthetic generator, I'm designing strikes around the spot price with a step size proportional to spot, using a lognormal decay model centered at slightly different anchors for calls and puts to create realistic skew, plus random "walls" at a few strikes for volatility clustering — all seeded for reproducibility.

Now running the inversion and validation to extract the embedded dataset and compute statistics, then deciding on the default spot price: rather than claiming a specific real price, I'll use a neutral default like 245 with a label indicating it's adjustable and should be calibrated by the user. After validation, building out the app interface to display the option chain and metrics.

For the charts, I'm setting up the pain curve with three series (total, call, put) in different colors, adding reference lines for the current pin and initial spot, and overlaying a what-if scenario when active. The domain switches between focused and full view, the y-axis uses linear scaling with compact formatting, and on hover I'll show the payoff breakdown including what the seller would receive at that settlement price.

The OI bars chart displays call and put open interest symmetrically around a center zero line, with the y-axis scaled to ±1.1× the max OI. Clicking a bar selects that strike (or the nearest one with OI), highlighting it via the bar stroke, and the readout shows the hovered strike's call and put OI values.

For controls, I'm adding a side segment toggle for calls vs puts, a strike selector (either via clicking the OI chart or a dropdown menu), and a delta OI slider ranging from −50k to +200k that recalculates the pain curve in real-time and displays the change as a ghost overlay on both charts. There's also a leverage hint text element, and the top of the pain chart card shows a summary strip with the pain point, minimum loss value, total call OI, and total put OI.

The data state tracks the current spot price, contract multiplier, focus mode, the option rows with strikes and open interest, and the selected side with strike and delta offset. I'm implementing pain calculation functions that iterate through the rows to sum call and put losses at any given price point, then computing all strikes sorted for the table display. Hovering on either chart syncs the settlement price axis across both, and the number formatting includes comma separators.

For the parser, I'm splitting input on whitespace or delimiters, skipping headers if they contain NaN, requiring at least 3 columns, and falling back to deriving contract volume from open interest if the volume column is missing—the paste format optionally includes volumes in columns 4 and 5. I'm also adding a synthetic random number generator, implementing a whatif overlay in the second chart as a ghost bar at the selected strike extended by the delta offset with a dashed outline, and then cross-checking the convexity claim against real data to see if there are any flat segments where consecutive totals are equal.

sections.text:
All the recovered OI values check out as exact integers with zero discrepancy between the cached table and recomputed values. Max pain sits at 250, and the overall structure shows 112,982 calls against 86,013 puts for a PCR of 0.761. The open interest is heavily concentrated in the 135–350 range with pronounced walls at 250, 252.5, and 255 on the call side and 250, 247.5 on the put side—a textbook pin setup. There's a notable valley at 242.5 with 574k contracts and another dip at 250 with 289k.

Now I'm moving into the web app build. The design is locked in: charts will focus on the 135–350 active region with a toggle to view the full 70–350 range. The console includes a spot price slider (150–350, defaulting to 245), a per-share versus notional toggle, a focus toggle between valley and full domain, and a dataset name chip. The core interaction is an OI injection what-if tool rather than a separate animation. I'm structuring five main cards: the pain curve with dashboard stats and what-if overlay, an OI terrain bar chart for strike selection, a magnetic absorption experiment card with controls and live results, a prose card for methodology and critique, and a data entry section with paste, synthetic generation, and restore options. I'll reuse the existing engine and add bar chart functionality with click handlers to drive the what-if overlays.

For the pain calculation, I'm writing a function that evaluates the pain curve at each strike in the grid, returning key metrics like the minimum loss point and total pain. The what-if logic clones the current dataset, adjusts the selected strike's OI by a delta amount, recomputes the pain, and overlays the new total on the original chart in a dashed terra color while showing a ghost bar extension on the OI chart. A strike selector dropdown pulls from the current dataset and can be set by clicking the bar chart. The OI delta slider ranges from −30,000 to +60,000 with a 500-unit step, clamping to ensure OI never goes negative.

Now I'm setting up the readout displays: the main pain readout shows the maximum pain strike and total pain in contracts and notional dollars, with a hover state showing the seller's payout at any given price level and the distance from the valley. The second readout displays the hovered strike's OI for calls and puts with a prompt to select it for the what-if experiment. The third readout shows the result of the injection—the new pain point after adding OI at a specific strike.

For the stats display, I'm using dashboard tiles to show these metrics. On the formatting side, I need to handle thousands separators for readability—I'll use a custom function with regex to add commas to numbers rather than relying on locale-specific formatting, which keeps things consistent across environments.

For the display values themselves, I'm multiplying by a unit multiplier (either 1 or 100) depending on whether we're showing per-share values or nominal dollar amounts, then appending the appropriate label. The y-axis needs compact formatting too—values in the millions get abbreviated with an 'M' suffix, and thousands with a 'k'.

On the domain side, I'm calculating the focus domain based on strikes where there's actual payoff (where calls plus puts are greater than zero), then padding it by one step on either side. The x-axis ticks should land on nice round numbers across the continuous range.

For the bar widths, I'm computing the spacing between consecutive strikes in the view—using tighter spacing near the money (2.5 units) and wider spacing elsewhere (5 units)—then setting each bar's width to 80% of the minimum gap to its neighbors. I'm also adding a dashed line to mark the spot price S₀ with a label.

The prose sections are structured in three parts: first covering definitions and convexity proofs, including a note about a code comment I found that showed the original author had already caught and corrected their thinking about where maximum loss occurs; second covering the mechanics and walls; third continuing into the final section.

Now I'm moving into the criticisms and empirical evidence—pulling in the Ni–Pearson–Poteshman 2005 paper that documented price clustering around option strikes on expiration dates, with mechanisms involving market maker delta hedging and possible manipulation, though the effect size is small. I'm also noting modern caveats: the dilution from 0DTE options, the distinction between open interest and net writer position, and the important caveat that max pain shouldn't be treated as a price prediction but rather as a prior. I'm also contrasting this with gamma exposure work—both tend to point toward adjacent strikes during monthly expirations, but the causal mechanisms differ: max pain only looks at settlement transfers, while gamma exposure looks at dynamic hedging flows.

The thinking then shifts to treating max pain as a terrain map rather than a navigation tool, then moves into describing a data input interface with a textarea for option chain data (supporting strike price, call/put open interest, and optionally volumes), buttons for applying pasted data and generating synthetic chains, controls for adjusting current price and skew parameters, and a status line. There's also mention of how the max pain calculation translates from the Python backend to JavaScript, with a double loop structure that evaluates each strike price.

The data sources flow from the Futu API pipeline (noting the web interface can't connect directly), the Excel workbook with three sheets mapping to different sections of the interface, and helper scripts that log date checks. The console outputs the top 10 results with hover details and valley neighborhood visualization. There's a note about a data discrepancy where the control panel shows an incomplete 10-10 date from a previous run, but the actual chain data and pain analysis table both use the 10-17 monthly expiration.

Now I'm setting up the page title and structure for the max pain visualization — it'll display the GOOGL 2025-10-17 real open interest data with the pain curve and magnetic attraction experiment, sourced from the Futu pipeline and rendered as a static terrain map. I'm designing the card glyphs using monospace font styling with ASCII-compatible symbols to represent summation, open interest, and magnetic concepts.

Building the visualization engine... Then I'll run the test suite: sanity checks on the what-if logic, parser validation, synthetic data generation for determinism, and jsdom smoke tests to verify the charts render and interactions work—since getBoundingClientRect returns zero, I'll trigger select and slider events directly instead of click simulation, test the focus and multiplier toggles, and simulate paste by setting the textarea value and clicking apply. Finally, I'll use cairosvg to visually verify the pin line sits at the 250 position, bars are mirrored correctly, and the valley minimum aligns at 250.

Now I'm setting up the JavaScript with the embedded Google stock dataset, implementing the pain calculation algorithm, and wiring together the chart engine with pain and open interest visualizations, plus the what-if scenario controls for strike selection and delta adjustments. Scaling the y-axis values by the multiplier directly so the axis reads in the chosen unit, then adding chart references like a gold pin for the max pain point, a dashed line for S₀, and a terra-colored pin for the new pain point if there's a what-if scenario. I'll also add a dot at the pain/minLoss intersection and make the readout interactive—hovering shows the nearest strike, while the continuous display interpolates linearly across the piecewise linear pain curve to show settlement outcomes at any price point compared to the valley value.

For the bars chart, I'm calculating bar widths as 72% of the minimum gap to neighboring strikes, with call OI extending upward and put OI downward, then highlighting the selected strike with a darker outline and adding a dashed ghost rectangle for what-if scenarios showing the effective change.

For rendering, I'm creating SVG rectangles positioned at each strike's center with heights matching the OI values, using event delegation on the chart level to detect clicks and snap to the nearest strike rather than attaching listeners to individual bars.

The hover readout displays the nearest strike's call and put OI with a note indicating whether it's selected, and there's a sync group mechanism being set up.

Now I'm wiring the what-if panel: populating a dropdown with strike options showing their call and put OI values, adding side toggles and a slider for position delta with a display showing the signed change, and handling the clear action to reset the delta while optionally keeping or clearing the selected strike.

The result text updates dynamically based on what's selected—if both strike and delta are set, it shows the projected pain point and movement range; if only the strike is chosen, it prompts to adjust the slider. Clicking an OI value in the chart syncs the dropdown selection, and I'm also building a parser that tokenizes input lines and skips header rows. When the dataset changes, I'll adjust the S₀ slider range dynamically based on the pain values—setting the minimum to around 80% of the lowest strike and maximum to 120% of the highest. For synthetic data generation, I'm using a seeded random number generator and calculating strike spacing based on the spot price, then creating a range around that spot with appropriate snapping. The open interest distribution uses exponential decay functions centered near the spot price with different spreads for calls and puts, scaled by predefined amplitude levels.

I'm also building out the UI controls: a reset button that restores the default GOOGL data and clears all modifications, handlers for the multiplier and focus segments, formatting functions to display large numbers with appropriate suffixes (billions, millions, thousands), and a unit name function that switches between nominal dollar amounts and share quantities based on the multiplier setting.

Now I'm refining the charting engine itself — stripping it down to just the essential components like the grid, reference lines, data series, bars, legend, readout display, and crosshair interaction. For the pain curve interpolation across the full domain, I'm using piecewise linear interpolation at the strike points, which gives exact values. The hover interaction clamps to the valid domain, and anything beyond the outermost strikes gets handled gracefully. The readout uses direct calculation rather than interpolation to avoid edge cases.

Setting the chart dimensions: pain curve at 430 pixels tall, options impact chart at 400 pixels.

For the final assembly, I'm concatenating three pieces together — the opening script tag and setup code, the embedded data from the GOOGL rows file, and the main charting logic — using a build script that pipes everything into the output file.

sections.text:
**核心判断：原程序是一条实时管道（富途 API → 双重循环 → Excel 三表），网页连不上行情网关，所以这次"做成 web 程序"的正解是把管道铸成静物——算法逐式复刻、真实数据内置、数据入口换成剪贴板。** 三份作品至此成一个序列：Greeks 曲面画"场"、Long Call 画"个体"、这份画"群体"。

这次逆向里有个值得一说的发现：工作簿的「期权数据」表 OI 列全为零（控制面板状态冻结在"正在获取期权链..."——一次中断的运行），但「痛点分析」表完好。由于总痛函数是分段线性、折点在行权价上，**对缓存损益曲线做二阶差分即可精确反演出 OI 阶梯**——73 档全部还原为非负整数，正向复算与缓存表 219 个数值逐分不差（残差=0），痛点 $250 与 B4 单元格一致。于是 GOOGL 2025-10-17 的真实持仓（含 $252.5 的 30,689 张 Call 墙、$250 的 22,280 张 Put 墙，PCR 0.761）以 920 字节内置成默认数据集。

五个区块：

**壹·痛点曲线**——总痛 + Call/Put 分解三线，谷底钉标。prose 里写明了两个技术点：只在行权价上取值不是近似（凸的分段线性函数最小值必在折点），以及原码注释里那次"修正"方向自纠——这个概念确实容易绕晕，页面统一"卖方最省/买方最痛"双口径。

**贰·OI 双墙地形**——Call 朝上深青、Put 朝下赤陶的镜像柱图，痛点与 S₀ 参考线贯穿。**点击任意柱即选中该行权价**。

**叁·磁吸实验**（本页签名交互）——选方向、选行权价、拖 ΔOI 滑杆，壹图实时叠加实验后总痛曲线与新痛点。已验证的例子：$255 注入 +20,000 张 Put，痛点即从 $250 拉到 $252.5；而想把针拽出谷区要贵一个数量级——凸谷底部平坦、谷壁陡峭，就是"磁吸"的数学本体。负注入自动截断于现有持仓。

**肆·口径与批评**——诚实的部分：pinning 有文献（Ni–Pearson–Poteshman 2005）；经不起的部分：OI≠净裸卖方、真正的日内压力来自 Gamma 对冲流（你 gamma-atlas 的对象）而非这个会计极小点、0DTE 时代口径进一步稀释。结论一句话：地形图，不是导航仪。

**伍·数据入口**——粘贴任意券商导出的链（3–5 列，保留原程序的 OI→Volume 回退分支），或用合成生成器（现价锚/规模/Put偏斜，种子递增连点换地形）。粘贴自定义数据后 S₀ 滑杆范围自适应。

复刻表里也如实记了两处原件瑕疵：B2 到期日停在未完成运行的 10-10（数据实为 10-17），以及那张全零 OI 表的诊断。

试一个动作：点贰图 $255 那根次高的 Call 墙 → 叁里切到 Put、推到 +20,000 → 看大头针跳一档；再切回 Call 推满 +80,000，看它为什么纹丝不动。

entries.title: 系统论视角下的德国古典哲学神学背景分析
entries.summary:
**Conversation overview**

The person engaged Claude in a two-stage intellectual task involving two Chinese documents on philosophy and systems theory. The first document ("蓝本") applied modern systems theory to analyze the developmental history of logic as a system, establishing a methodological framework using concepts drawn from Spencer-Brown, Maturana-Varela, Ashby, von Foerster, and Luhmann. The second document ("文本") surveyed the theological backgrounds of four German Classical philosophers: Kant, Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel. The person asked Claude to use the analytical methods from the first document as a lens through which to analyze and summarize the content of the second document, then to reformat the resulting analysis as a standard formal Word document.

The intellectual work involved translating the God-concept into systems theory language (as the personified storage of the closure dream), identifying Kant's critique of the three proofs of God as a structural analogue to Gödel's incompleteness result, and tracing how each subsequent philosopher—Fichte, Schelling, Hegel—represented an escalating attempt to refuse and overcome that impossibility verdict. The core thesis produced was that German Classical Idealism ran logic history's developmental arc in reverse: receiving its incompleteness judgment first (Kant, 1781) and then spending seventy years attempting to rebuild closure anyway, culminating in Hegel's maximal synthesis which immediately fractured into an interpretive ecology. Key systems theory concepts applied included: distinction operations, autopoiesis, requisite variety, re-entry, blind spots, deparadoxification, stratification, and open-system ecology. The person's established philosophical orientation—treating paradox as exposing the limits of observational tools rather than as a feature of Being itself, and preferring Wittgenstein-Gödel-Tarski over Hegelian approaches—shaped the analytical framing throughout.

For the Word document deliverable, Claude used the docx Node.js library to generate a formally structured Chinese document with: a centered title block in 黑体 at 22pt with a 楷体 subtitle and date, a prefatory 编制说明 paragraph defining the two source documents and listing methodological tools, seven numbered first-level headings in 黑体 at 16pt, body text in 宋体 at 12pt with 1.5× line spacing and two-character first-line indentation, a five-column comparison table (表1) with parchment-toned header shading comparing the four philosophers across five dimensions, and centered page-number footers. The document was converted to PDF for visual verification before delivery. Second-person references from the conversational analysis ("你的立场") were neutralized to objective references to the 蓝本 throughout the formal document.
